extracted.intended_audience: literary readers, critics, playwrights, poets, and translators (informed general readers of literary criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading literary criticism addressing how to evaluate and produce stage-plays, dramatic spectacle, dialogue, poetry, and translations (with examples from Kotzebue, Klopstock, Milton, and German verse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness/realism of stage spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: "a little real gunpowder being set fire to ... the naturalness of the scene was quite astonishing!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory, concrete effects (smell, sound, real props) to increase the naturalness of a scene; stage realism can produce strong audience astonishment and emotional engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity / elevation through fate and grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: "that dependence of thousands on the fate of one ... gives so lofty an interest to the personages of Shakspcarc, and the Greek Tragedians"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic interest may be heightened by invoking large-scale stakes and the power of destiny or divine agency; such elevation lifts characters and creates profound emotional effect (the 'sublimest of all feelings').

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of contemporary human wants and passions
rubrics_metrics.description: "We seek and find on the present stage our own wants and passions, our own vexations, losses, and embarrassments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plays that mirror present-day, relatable human concerns can be valuable; judge works for how they reflect and satisfy current social/emotional needs, rather than only for timeless grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatricality vs. dramatic (literary) genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Kotzebue 'theatrical rather than a dramatic; genius, and hence its products were in their nature transitory'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between theatrical skill (scene-painting, spectacle, immediate stage effect) and enduring dramatic/literary value; theatrical mastery may produce transient popular success even if not 'permanent' literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of stage effect / pictorial spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Kotzebue was 'as great a master of stage-effect ... and was as warm an enthusiast in his lower vocation ... a great scene-painter'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate spectacle pieces by their pictorial effect, fertility, mutability, and capacity to display actors and stirring adventure; compare such works to visual art (e.g., Rubens) rather than to high tragic literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral content and ethical influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of whether Kotzebue's plays were 'wholly immoral' or 'upon the brink of moral licentiousness' and whether they 'paint more disinterestedly virtuous characters'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plays for their moral tendencies: do they corrupt or elevate moral feeling? Consider whether vice is glorified or whether virtuous characters receive dignified approbation; compare with more corrosive productions when judging ethical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liveliness of dialogue and appeal to sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taylor praises 'the liveliness of his dialogue, and its "bold-appeal to the fairest sentiments and dearest feelings of our nature"'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge dialogue on its vivacity and its capacity to rouse sentiments; lively, appealing dialogue can be a strong merit even if the play is theatrical rather than literary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate plays by their intended medium (performance vs. reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: "They were never that; it was as though we should transport a clever scene-piece into a picture-gallery, or spell out at home a popular preacher's sermon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate spectacle-driven plays solely as closet texts; many stage pieces must be judged by their live effect and performance context rather than by isolated reading of the printed dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of literary comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Taylor's parallels (e.g., comparing Schiller/Goethe to others) as sometimes like 'comparing Paradise Lost to the Prophecies of Isaiah'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid false or inapt comparisons between unlike authors/works; judge each work within its genre, purpose, and scale rather than by inappropriate parallels to masterpieces of a different kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic rhythm: arrangement of pauses, cadences, and paragraphic sweep
rubrics_metrics.description: "harmonious verse ... consisted ... in the apt arrangement of pauses and cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging verse (especially blank verse), assess the placement of pauses and cadences and the larger paragraphic movement; the musical and rhetorical flow across lines and stanzas is crucial to poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-specific expressive power / condensation (German)
rubrics_metrics.description: Klopstock's claim that German possesses a 'superior power of concentrating meaning' and that German can often express in one line what takes more in English
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing poetry and translation, account for language-specific features (compounding, prefixed participles) that allow greater density and picturesque unity in German; recognize that such structural advantages affect original composition and translation choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of morphological resources (compound verbs, prefixes) to condense meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation of German prefixed participles (ver-, zer-, ent-, etc.) and how they allow fine distinctions and condensation: e.g., revsen to rend, verreissen to rend away, zerreissen to rend to pieces
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and value morphological tools that permit condensations of meaning; in translation or composition, be aware of what is gained or lost when such compact expressions lack direct equivalents in the target language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and faithfulness in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint that English translations of Klopstock's Messiah had 'pages on pages, not in the original: — and half the original was not to be found in the translation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations should avoid adding, omitting, or inventing material; fidelity to the original's content and spirit is a critical standard (render select passages as faithful specimens rather than expansive paraphrase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosodic and quantitative differences in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: "three English lines will express four lines German" and comment that English has more monosyllables while German is polysyllabic
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for prosodic differences—line length, syllabic structure, and metre—when translating verse; literal one-to-one line rendering is often impossible and can misrepresent the original's rhythm and density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about imitating great models (Milton)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The reader of Milton must be always on his duty ... A man must have his sense to imitate him worthily."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When emulating a towering style, exercise caution: imitation can overpower a weaker poet, producing 'overflavored' works; maintain originality and the reader's ability to distinguish reproduction from genuine voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and quality of similes and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where Glover's similes are 'flattened' or 'mangled' Miltonic passages (quoted examples)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge similes and imagery for freshness and aptness; borrowed or mechanical echoes of a prior master result in flatness rather than poetic force—ensure comparisons are vivid and not mere slavish adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of descriptive scenes (light/shade segmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual description of sunset where 'trees ... were cut or divided into equal segments of deep shade and brassy light' producing a 'fairy scene'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts of light and shade, measured segmentation, and selective obscurity to create romantic or fairy-like visual effects; careful compositional choices (what to render obscure vs. illuminated) magnify pictorial and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of authorial/personal presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that Klopstock's powdered periwig 'enormously injured the effect of his physiognomy' and 'The author of The Messiah should have worn his own grey hair.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how an author's personal presentation or public persona affects reception; affectations of fashion or artifice can wound the reader's sense of naturalness and authenticity—simplicity may better suit venerable authors.
